The average is $705 for a one-carat lab-grown diamond. The offers underneath it run from $185 to $3,247 — a spread of 17.6 times.

CaratRadar's reference has fallen for four straight readings this month: $727, $711, $707, $705, down 3.03% in six days — a slow decline, not the collapse the category is usually described with. But the number underneath the number is the one worth carrying: the same page averaging $705 shows one-carat rounds offered at a quarter of that and at four and a half times it. At two carats the range runs $345 to $6,984; at three, $449 to $12,050.

A second source disagrees. This paper's own six-retailer sample, taken 25 July, priced the same stone at $550 — 28.2% below today's reference. Neither figure is wrong. There is no clearing exchange behind either one to settle the question.

Natural diamonds have Rapaport. Lab-grown has aggregator averages that disagree by 28% and ranges that disagree by seventeen-fold, and the gap is not error — it's cut quality, growth method and brand pretending to be the same product. The useful number for a retailer is not $705. It's the range.

Shanghai gold rose 1.41% today. China's jewellery counter rose 1.52%. The margin between them moved fifteen hundredths of a point.

The Shanghai Gold Exchange's Au99.99 closed at 954.01 yuan a gram today, up 13.29 yuan on the session. Chow Tai Fook's counter read 1,332 yuan, a figure two independent Chinese aggregators agree on. Divide one by the other and the shop window sits 39.62% above the exchange — against 39.47% three days ago, when this paper printed 940.72 and 1,312.

That is the test this desk set on 14 August: that China's counter price is a merchant setting a margin, not a market clearing. Three sessions have now returned the answer the argument predicted. The shop moved the same percentage the metal did, not the same number of yuan — and a 1.4% rally that would cut a fixed-yuan margin instead left this one exactly where it was.

The number to watch is still the 39.6%, not the 1,332. A margin that survives a 1.4% move in the underlying is a decision somebody is defending.

No edition published on 15 or 16 August. This morning the tape caught up — and every metal on it is higher than the last mark this paper printed.

Kitco's board at 05:59 New York time read gold $4,394.60, silver $65.38, platinum $1,749.00 and palladium $1,311.00. Against the exchange's own prior close, that's a single session's move — gold up $19.00. Against this paper's last printed tape, from 14 August, it's three days deep — gold up $38.40, or 0.88%. Both numbers are on the page, because a reader taking the smaller one at face value would think gold moved half of what it actually did.

Palladium carries the sharper story. The mark being retired, $1,297.00, was set on 14 August and held through two mornings this desk found it disagreed with the market — then this morning, four independent pages read between $1,311.00 and $1,351.00, every one of them above the held mark. Three sessions of holding a number, while four pages print higher ones, is an old number with a procedure wrapped around it.
